Peter Henseler and Johann Kroha
Physikalisches Institut, Universit¨at Bonn, Nußallee 12, D-53115 Bonn, Germany

Boris Shapiro
Department of Physics, Technion-Israel Institute of Technology, Haifa 32000, Israel

We study the suppression of electron localization due to the screening of disorder in a Hubbard-
Anderson model. We focus on the change of the electron localization length at the Fermi level within
a static picture, where interactions are absorbed into the redeﬁnition of the random on-site energies.
Two diﬀerent approximations are presented, either one yielding a nonmonotonic dependence of the
localization length on the interaction strength, with a pronounced maximum at an intermediate
interaction strength. In spite of its simplicity, our approach is in good agreement with recent
numerical results.

PACS numbers: 71.10.Fd, 73.20.Fz, 72.15.Rn, 71.30.+h

I. INTRODUCTION

Understanding the interplay between disorder and
electron-electron interactions remains one of the major
challenges in modern condensed matter physics, experi-
mental as well as theoretical. The research in this ﬁeld
has been stimulated by the possible metallic behavior
in two-dimensional disordered interacting systems.1 A
metallic phase at zero temperature in two or less dimen-
sions would be in contrast to the prediction of the scaling
theory of Anderson localization.2 The possible existence
of a metallic phase, induced by interactions, is a long
standing3 and still controversial problem, discussed by
many authors during the last three decades.4

One of the ideas proposed and discussed by several au-
thors is that interactions lead to a partial screening of the
random potential and, thus, reduce the eﬀect of local-
ization. In particular, the 2d disordered Hubbard model
(the Hubbard-Anderson model) has been studied, mostly
numerically, and it was demonstrated that repulsive in-
teractions can have a delocalizing eﬀect.5,6,7,8,9,10,11

In this paper, we present an analytical study of the
screening eﬀect, focussing on the case of strong disor-
der at zero temperature, when the Hubbard-Anderson
model is in the regime of an Anderson insulator. Our
approach is based on an exact treatment of the atomic
limit, followed by ”switching on” the intersite hopping t,
under the assumption that the atomic-limit occupation
numbers do not change. Let us emphasize that in our
static approach, the interactions only change the original
on-site energies. Therefore, we are left with a single-
particle Anderson Hamiltonian, and the question is how
the localized single-particle states may change due to the
new, renormalized probability distribution of the on-site
energies. In this sense, the approach is close, although
not identical, to the Hartree-Fock treatment. A compar-
ison of both methods will be presented. Although this
approach is formulated for an arbitrary ﬁlling factor, it
becomes inadequate close to half ﬁlling where magnetic
eﬀects dominate12 (such eﬀects are not considered in our

work).
Furthermore, we will show that, for ﬁxed disorder, the
localization length ξ is a nonmonotonic function of the
Hubbard interaction energy U, with a maximum for some
intermediate value of U. This is because for strong
interactions, the Mott-Hubbard physics of interaction-
suppressed hopping dominates, leading to the forma-
tion of two disorder broadened Hubbard bands with
a reduced average density of states at the Fermi level
and, as a consequence, increasing eﬀectively the disor-
der strength. In spite of the simplicity of the approach,
the results are in good agreement with recent numerical
studies,5,7,8,9,10,13,14 in the appropriate range of parame-
ters.
The evaluation of the localization length within our

A handful of documents substantively address Coulomb interaction involving electrons, in quite different physical settings.

## Answer: "Coulomb interaction electrons" across the corpus

The corpus treats the Coulomb interaction of electrons in four distinct contexts. No single document is "the" answer — they address different physics.

### 1. Electrons on a sphere — the Thomson problem (most direct match)
**Document `0707.3690.pdf`, pp. 5–6.** This paper (on virus-capsid geometry / generalized "CK" constructions) invokes the classic **Thomson problem**: "determining the minimum energy configuration for a collection of electrons constrained to move on the surface of a sphere and interacting via the Coulomb potential" (p. 5). The Coulomb repulsion drives the electrons into a triangular (hexagonal) lattice on the sphere, "where each electron has 6 nearest neighbors sitting at the vertices of an hexagon, with the exception of 12 locations" — the topologically required disclination defects, which become pentagons ("there are only 5 sitting at the vertices of a pentagon… the icosadeltahedron," p. 6). The paper also notes generalizations to non-Coulomb repulsive potentials (the "generalized Thomson problem," p. 6). This is the corpus's clearest, most literal treatment of electrons interacting through the Coulomb potential.

### 2. Electron–electron interaction in disordered lattices — screening & localization
**Document `0707.1301.pdf` ("Static Screening and Delocalization Effects in the Hubbard-Anderson Model"), p. 1 (and refs p. 6).** Here the electron–electron interaction enters as the **on-site Hubbard repulsion** term `He-e = U Σ nᵢ↑nᵢ↓` in the Hamiltonian (Eq. 1, p. 1). The paper studies how this repulsion **screens the random disorder potential**, suppressing Anderson localization: the localization length is a *non-monotonic* function of the Hubbard interaction strength U, peaking at intermediate U before Mott-Hubbard physics takes over (p. 1). The bibliography (p. 6, ref. 11) points explicitly to models with **long-range Coulomb interactions** (Nemeth & Pichard). So this is the "electron–electron Coulomb interaction" story in condensed matter, modeled as an on-site Hubbard U.

### 3. Coulomb interaction between conjugated-polymer chains
**Document `0802.0539.pdf` (DFT study of PTV conjugated polymers), pp. 2–4.** Electronic-structure context: it stresses describing "both short (covalent) and long range (Coulomb and van der Waals) components of intermolecular interactions" (p. 2), and finds that "only Coulombic interaction, providing [the] most important contribution to the interchain interaction, is included" (pp. 3–4). The interchain Coulomb interaction splits the polymer's electronic states, reducing the bandgap and creating additional states (p. 4). Here Coulomb interaction shapes the electronic band structure of the material.

### 4. Coulomb losses of cosmic-ray particles to the thermal (electron) gas
**Document `2607.06744.pdf` ("CRexit observed: probing cosmic ray transport…"), p. 3.** In an astrophysics/plasma context, cosmic rays "exchange energy with the thermal gas" through "direct Coulomb and hadronic losses" (i.e., Coulomb collisions with the thermal electrons/ions), alongside indirect Alfvén-wave heating. This is Coulomb interaction involving charged particles and the thermal electron plasma, rather than bound/lattice electrons.

### Bibliographic-only mention
**Document `0904.1520.pdf`, p. 54** contains only a *reference* — Rozenbaum, "Coulomb interactions in two-dimensional lattice structures," Phys. Rev. B 53, 6240 (1996) — with no substantive discussion in the matched text.

---

**Bottom line:** If you want electrons interacting *through* the Coulomb potential in the literal sense, **`0707.3690.pdf` pp. 5–6 (Thomson problem)** is the answer. For electron–electron interaction as many-body condensed-matter physics, **`0707.1301.pdf` p. 1** (Hubbard U screening disorder). For Coulomb interaction governing material electronic structure, **`0802.0539.pdf` pp. 2–4**. For plasma/astrophysical Coulomb energy loss, **`2607.06744.pdf` p. 3**.

*Caveat:* the server's semantic search extra (`fastembed`) is not installed, so this ran as keyword-only search. A semantically-phrased hit (e.g., papers discussing electron correlation without the exact word "Coulomb") could be missed; the four documents above are those where the keyword actually appears in substantive text.
